newsitem.title: ALBANIA: International troops guard Albania's vote count.
newsitem.headline: International troops guard Albania's vote count.

text.p: International troops moved in to guard the headquarters of Albania's vote count on Friday, a day after a man was killed during a royalist rally outside the electoral commission.

With only two days to go to a second run-off round of voting, the failure of the Albanian authorities to declare a final result of last Sunday's first round was clearly testing the patience of international monitors.

Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current chairman of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe which is overseeing the vote, threatened on Thursday to block aid to Europe's poorest country unless all sides cooperated in the democratic process.
The secretary of the electoral commission, Thimio Kondi, told Reuters final results of the first round were expected later on Friday.

According to preliminary results, the opposition Socialists are heading for a crushing victory in the vote, which was called to end months of violence and anarchy following the collapse of savings schemes earlier this year.
Berisha has already conceded victory and has promised to honour an earlier pledge to step down once final results confirm that his Democratic Party has been beaten.

Earlier results showed the Socialists winning 49 of the 115 seats being contested by a straight majority vote, compared to eight for Berisha's Democrats. Sunday's run-off ballot will involve some 30 districts where no side won a majority in the first round.
Members of the multinational force sent to Albania to restore order took up positions around the Central Electoral Commission in central Tirana for the first time since last Sunday's vote.
Their deployment followed a rally outside the building on Thursday led by self-proclaimed king Leka which erupted into shooting in which one man was killed and two injured.
The royalists were protesting against what they said was fraud in a referendum held alongside last Sunday's vote, in which voters rejected restoration of the monarchy.
The firing started as Leka, dressed in battle fatigues and sporting two pistols on his belt, approached the building after marching with some 500 supporters from the central Skanderbeg square.
Monarchists said police started the shooting, but police denied this. Officials inside the building said the first shots came from the protesters.
The royalists vowed to stage another demonstration starting in Skanderbeg square on Friday evening.
However, police issued a statement warning that the country was still under a state of emergency which banned demonstrations unless they were authorised.
A spokesman for Leka's entourage said that he might attend the rally, scheduled for 7 p.m. (1700 GMT), depending on the turnout.
Justice Minister Spartak Ndjela told a news conference on Friday he had launched an investigation into who was responsible for the violence at Thursday's ill-fated rally.
